lookForward.fits: The Wild Card round ends tonight, 1 October 2026; the Division Series begin Saturday 3 October.
lookForward.headline: Baseball's next round starts Saturday
lookForward.line: The wild card games finish tonight. The Division Series begin Saturday, best of five. On television, and free on local radio. Pick a team you have no stake in and follow it to the end. It costs nothing and lasts three weeks.

source.name: MLB: 2026 Playoff and World Series schedule

more: The postseason works like this. Twelve teams get in, six from each league. The top two in each league sit out the first round; the other eight play best-of-three Wild Card Series, which started Tuesday and end tonight. The winners go on to the Division Series, best of five, starting Saturday 3 October.

After that come the League Championship Series, best of seven, from Sunday 11 October, and the World Series from Friday 23 October. Games run late on the east coast; the first pitch of a weekend afternoon game is the civilised way in.

Watching costs nothing if you have a radio. Every club broadcasts its games on a local station, and postseason games are carried nationally too. Radio is the better medium for baseball anyway: the pace suits a voice, and you can cook, walk or drive through it.

If you have no team, borrow one for three weeks. Pick the city you would most like to visit, or the team that has waited longest, and follow it through October. You will know four names by the weekend and have opinions by Tuesday. When they lose, and they probably will, it costs you nothing but a pleasant three weeks of autumn evenings.

goodThing.fits: The first days of October are among the biggest nights of the autumn bird migration over the United States.
goodThing.headline: Hundreds of millions of birds are crossing tonight
goodThing.line: Radar counts them. On the biggest nights this month, hundreds of millions cross after dark. Switch off an outdoor light; it helps them pass.

source.name: BirdCast, Cornell Lab of Ornithology: live migration maps

more: Most songbirds migrate at night. They leave about half an hour after sunset, climb to a few thousand feet, and fly until the small hours, navigating by stars, by the earth's magnetic field, and by landmarks below. In daylight they drop into whatever park, hedge or garden is underneath to eat and sleep.

Weather radar picks them up. The same dishes that watch for rain see the sky fill with birds after dusk, and researchers at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology turned that into BirdCast: live maps and nightly forecasts, county by county, of how many birds are in the air over the United States. On the biggest nights of the season the national total runs into the hundreds of millions.

Light is the problem. Birds flying at night are drawn off course by lit buildings, and the ones that survive the collisions burn energy circling a city instead of travelling. Turning lights off between midnight and dawn, closing a blind, or pointing a porch light down rather than up measurably reduces the toll.
Tomorrow morning, look in the nearest patch of trees. Some of tonight's travellers will be in it, tired and hungry, for one day only.

onThisDay.fits: 1 October 1890: Congress made Yosemite a national park.
onThisDay.headline: Yosemite became a national park
onThisDay.line: Congress set aside the high country around the valley: meadows, waterfalls and groves of giant sequoias. John Muir had spent two years writing to persuade them.

source.name: National Park Service: Yosemite enabling legislation

funFact.fits: 1 October 1908: Ford introduced the Model T.
funFact.reveal: Cars had existed for twenty years. What he did, with the Model T introduced on this day in 1908, was build one an ordinary family could afford.

source.name: The Henry Ford: Ford's Model T, a car for the great multitude

more: The Model T went on sale on 1 October 1908 at $850. It was not the first car, not the fastest and not the most comfortable, but it was light, simple, and built to survive roads that were mostly mud. A farmer could fix it with the tools in his barn.

The price is the whole story. Ford kept redesigning the way the car was made rather than the car itself, and in 1913 he put the moving assembly line into the Highland Park plant in Michigan. The time to build one fell from twelve hours to about ninety minutes, and the price fell with it, year after year, until a new Model T cost a few hundred dollars and a worker on Ford's own line could buy one.
Fifteen million were sold before production ended in 1927. The country rearranged itself around them: paved roads, filling stations, roadside diners, motels, weekends away.
The famous line about color came later, when black was the only paint that dried fast enough for the line. Early cars came in grey, green, blue and red.

calmRead.fits: Expands today's On this day: Yosemite becomes a national park, 1 October 1890.
calmRead.title: The meadows somebody wrote letters about
calmRead.teaser: A hundred and thirty-six years ago today, an argument about sheep made a national park.
paragraphs: Yosemite Valley had been protected since 1864, when Lincoln signed it over to the state of California to be kept for the public. But the valley is a small thing, about one percent of what we now call the park: the high country above it, the meadows where the rivers start, the groves of giant sequoias, all of that was open ground, and every summer it filled with sheep.

John Muir called them hoofed locusts. He had walked the Sierra Nevada for twenty years and watched the flocks crop the meadows to dust. In the summer of 1889 he took Robert Underwood Johnson, editor of a popular magazine in New York, camping at Tuolumne Meadows. By the campfire Johnson suggested the obvious thing: write it down, and I will print it.

Muir wrote two long articles that ran in 1890, full of waterfalls and cathedral rocks and the damage being done. Johnson lobbied Congress. On 1 October 1890 a bill passed setting aside the high country as a national park, the third in the country.

It took until 1906 for California to hand the valley itself back, and the whole thing became one park. Today it is about twelve hundred square miles, ninety-five percent of it wilderness with no road at all.

October is the quiet month there: the falls are thin, the crowds are gone, the black oaks turn yellow. Wherever you are this morning, the meadows are still there because somebody sat down and wrote about them.

source.name: National Park Service: Yosemite enabling legislation

word.fits: The giant sequoia groves that Yosemite was made to protect, on the day it was made.
word.meaning: The giant redwood of the Sierra Nevada. Named for Sequoyah, the Cherokee silversmith who invented a written alphabet for his language.

kindness.fits: The peak of the night bird migration.
kindness.text: Turn off one outside light tonight, or close the blind on a bright window. Birds are passing over your roof in the dark, and they steer by the sky.

joke.fits: The Model T, introduced on this day in 1908.
joke.setup: Why was the Model T such a good listener?
joke.punchline: It came in any color you liked, as long as it agreed with you.

riddle.fits: The giant sequoias of Yosemite, protected on this day in 1890.
riddle.riddle: I am older than every country on this continent, I am wider than a road, and my seed is smaller than an oat flake. What am I?
